open-question.question: The runner of Gurita for VS Code waits for a keypress after every chain and after every looped task run. A new setting is to close the terminal by itself when a chain ran all its lines. Does the setting also close the terminal of a looped task run that completed every task?
open-question.alternative: The one new setting governs both kinds of run. With it on, a looped task run that ends on `Loop finished: no task remains` (the runner's `finished` outcome, reached once no `##` heading is left in `TASKS_TODO.md`) prints its report and exits without waiting for a keypress, so its terminal closes and the page unblocks. A loop that stopped (an unresolved assignment, a task that did not end on `Task completed.`, or an unreadable task list) still waits for a keypress, as a stopped chain does. One rule for every run: `run_chain` and `run_loop` already end the same way (report, `wait_for_key`, exit 0 when finished), so the setting skips the same wait at both, and the looped run, which is the long unattended run where an unblocked page on success matters most, gets the benefit too. The loop's closing report (`Tasks completed: N`) and every task session's output vanish with the terminal on success, leaving only the commits and the refreshed page as the record; the setting's description and the README must say it reaches looped runs, since the tracker entry names only chains.

The setting closes only a chain's terminal. A looped task run keeps waiting for a keypress after its report whatever the setting says and however the loop ended, exactly as today. Follows the tracker entry's wording literally and keeps the one run that can complete many tasks unattended always reviewable at its end, with the runner's loop path left unchanged. A loop that completed every task still leaves the mission's page blocked until someone presses a key, the very wait the setting exists to remove, and a user who turned the setting on is likely to read the loop's lingering terminal as the setting not working.

Looped runs get a setting of their own beside the chain one: with it on, a looped task run that ends on `Loop finished: no task remains` exits without waiting for a keypress, while a stopped loop still waits; the chain setting does not reach loops and the loop setting does not reach chains. Lets a user auto-close short chains while still reviewing the output of a long multi-task run, or the reverse, without either choice being forced on the other. Adds a second setting to the manifest, its description, and the README for a distinction few users are likely to want, and needs a default of its own, which depends on how the default of the chain setting is settled.

open-question.question: No recipe in `gurita-vscode/shipped_recipes.md`, the recipe file Gurita for VS Code ships, holds a `codex` line, and the file is to gain one. Which shipped recipes gain a Codex line: a single-task line, one variant of one chain, or a Codex variant of several chains?
open-question.alternative: One new single-task recipe, `Single task (Codex)`, beside the three existing ones: one headless line `codex exec '$gurita:complete-task --mission <path> <Task Title>' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, in the form `docs/ways-of-using.md` gives, carrying no `-m`. No chain gains a variant and no button recipe changes. The smallest change that ships a Codex line. A `task_line_rules.txt` rule can send matching tasks of a looped run to Codex, the same way the Antigravity single-task line is used. The line is one task's run, in the headless form the 2026-11-22 check confirmed, and it runs on any Codex account because it names no model. A Codex user still has no chain to fire from a mission page, so every workflow step outside task completion stays Claude Code or Antigravity. With no `-m` on any shipped Codex line, the Settings window's Codex model list, which is read from `-m` on `codex` lines, gets nothing from the shipped file.

The same single `Single task (Codex)` recipe, its one headless `codex exec '$gurita:complete-task …' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` line also carrying `-m` with a named Codex model id. The recipe name says the model, as the Claude Code single-task names do. No chain or button recipe changes. As small as the account-default single-task line, and it also gives the Settings window's Codex model list a shipped entry. The shipped line then gets its own model dropdown, so Codex in the harness dropdown has a model to offer from the first run. It pins a model id that was not part of the 2026-11-22 check. That id can go stale or be unavailable on a given account, and the line then stops a run that would have worked at the account's default. Only task completion reaches Codex.

One chain gains one variant: `Execute tasks` gets a `Codex` variant holding one headless line, `codex exec '$gurita:complete-all-tasks --mission <path>' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, with no `-m`. Its two Claude Code variants stay interactive. No single-task recipe or other chain changes. A Codex user can fire it straight from the variant dropdown at the execute-tasks step. The chain is one skill, and the host suite has already seen it on Codex, dispatching complete-task agents through `spawn_agent` in rounds. A whole run can be handed to Codex without writing a rule file. The line is headless while its sibling variants are interactive, so the chain ends with no session left open. Its run, many agents under `agents.max_threads` rounds, is longer and less checked end to end than a single task. Codex reaches no step before execution, and no Codex line puts an entry in the Settings model list.

alternative.id: Mixed-agent variant with one Codex line

open-question.alternative: One chain gains one mixed-agent variant, on the pattern of the existing `Mixed-agent (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` variant. Exactly one of its lines is a headless `codex exec '$gurita:<skill> …' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` line with no `-m`, for example the alternatives pass in a `First run` variant, and the chain's other lines stay `claude` lines. No single-task recipe changes. It fits a pattern the shipped file already teaches, one harness taking one pass of a chain. It puts Codex where an independent second model adds the most, without asking a user to trust Codex with a whole chain. Running the variant needs two harnesses installed and signed in, so it is not a Codex-only path. Which chain and which pass to choose is a judgment the file then stands behind. If the chosen chain is `Requirements iteration`, the variant depends on how the lines of that renamed chain end up.

Every chain whose steps all have a headless form gains a `Codex` variant made only of `codex exec '$gurita:<skill> …' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` lines with no `-m`: `First run`, `Requirements iteration`, `Prepare tasks`, `Prepare and Execute tasks`, `Execute tasks`, and `Finish mission`. The chains that end on an interactive `claude` line get a headless Codex line there instead. A `Single task (Codex)` recipe of the same form stands beside them. Button recipes do not change. A Codex-only user can fire every workflow step from a mission page and send looped-run tasks to Codex. Codex then stands as a full third harness, matching the harness check and install support the extension already gives it. It adds the most to the shipped file: seven new variant blocks to keep in step with their Claude Code siblings. Only the single-line headless form has been checked, so whole chains, the review and recommendation passes among them, would ship unverified on Codex. The `Requirements iteration` variant depends on how the lines of that renamed chain end up. No line seeds the Settings model list.

alternative.id: Codex variants of several chains with model

open-question.alternative: The same full set: `Codex` variants of `First run`, `Requirements iteration`, `Prepare tasks`, `Prepare and Execute tasks`, `Execute tasks`, and `Finish mission`, plus a Codex single-task recipe. Every line is headless `codex exec '$gurita:<skill> …' --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` and carries `-m` with a named Codex model id, chosen per line as the Claude Code lines choose their families. Codex becomes a full third harness, and every shipped Codex line also has its own model dropdown. The Settings window's Codex model list starts filled from the shipped file, and the chains can give the heavy passes and the light ones different models, as the Claude Code chains do. The largest change and the most exposed to drift. Every line pins an id that no check has covered, so a model retired or missing on an account breaks every Codex chain at once. The `Requirements iteration` variant depends on how the lines of that renamed chain end up.

open-question.question: The recipe `Requirements iteration` that Gurita for VS Code ships is to be renamed "Approve all standing recommendations and review again". The old name also heads a recipe in `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md`, the hand-use document no tool reads. Is that recipe renamed there too?
open-question.alternative: The `### Requirements iteration` heading in `snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` is renamed to `### Approve all standing recommendations and review again` in this mission, in the same change that renames the shipped recipe. Only the heading changes: its `Stage: additional review round` line stays, the separate `### Mixed-agent requirements review (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` recipe beside it keeps its own name and form, and the file's other recipes are untouched. One chain carries one name across the repository. The listing README tells readers the snippet file holds "the same recipes" as the shipped file, so a reader moving between the button and the hand-use document finds the chain under the name the button shows. The edit is one line in a file no tool reads, so nothing can break. The edit reaches a root-level file outside the mission's `gurita-vscode/` scope, which is adjacent work, not core work. The snippet's mixed-agent chain stays a recipe of its own while the shipped file holds it as a variant of the renamed recipe, so the two documents still differ in shape. Whether the snippet's lines under the new heading still match its name depends on how the sibling question on the renamed chain's lines is settled.

The heading is renamed to `### Approve all standing recommendations and review again` as in the heading-only option, and the snippet's `### Mixed-agent requirements review (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` recipe moves under it as a second `####` variant, so the renamed recipe holds `#### default` and `#### Mixed-agent (Gemini reviews, Claude annotates)` as the shipped file does. The variant form is one the snippet file already describes in its `## Recipes` introduction and uses for `Execute tasks`. Every other recipe in the file stays as it is. The hand-use document then holds this chain in the same shape and under the same name as the shipped file, so the README's statement that it holds "the same recipes" is true for this chain, and a reader copying either variant by hand finds both under the one heading the button shows. It goes beyond renaming: it restructures a document no tool reads, outside the mission's scope and outside any tracker entry, and it removes a heading (`Mixed-agent requirements review …`) that hand users may know. The mixed-agent variant's lines differ from the default's in order and harness, so whether they still fit the new name depends on how the sibling question on the renamed chain's lines is settled.

`snippets/GURITA_USAGE.md` is not edited by this mission. Its `### Requirements iteration` recipe keeps its heading and lines, and only the shipped file, the extension's tests, the listing README, and the `CLAUDE.md` layout entry move to the new name. Any later rename is left to whoever next edits the hand-use document, and this mission plans none. The mission stays inside its `gurita-vscode/` scope and inside what the tracker asks for, which is a rename of the recipe Gurita for VS Code ships. The snippet file is read by no tool and the extension already does not mirror it (its mixed-agent chain is a separate recipe there and a variant in the shipped file), so leaving it changes no behaviour. The repository then names one chain two ways, and the listing README, which points readers to the snippet file as holding the same recipes, sends them to a document where the button's name does not appear. The mismatch persists with no task recording it, so it is likely to stay until someone notices.
